nameStory: The blue-winged teal gets its name from the brilliant sky-blue patches on its wings that flash like jewels when it takes flight. 'Teal' comes from the Middle English word for a small duck, and this species shows off those gorgeous blue wing coverts that make identification a snap once you see them in action.
description: The blue-winged teal is one of New England's smaller dabbling ducks, about the size of a pigeon but with a longer neck and broader body. Males sport a distinctive white crescent moon marking in front of their eye during breeding season, while both sexes have that telltale bright blue patch on their wings. These compact ducks have relatively large bills for their size and tend to sit lower in the water than larger ducks. They're early migrants, often among the first ducks to head south in late summer.

idTips.label: Blue wing patches
idTips.description: Brilliant sky-blue patches on the forewings are visible both in flight and when the duck stretches or flaps while on water - look for this electric blue color that seems almost artificial

idTips.label: White facial crescent
idTips.description: Breeding males show a bold white crescent or comma shape just in front of the eye, standing out sharply against their grayish head

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than mallards, with a relatively large, spatula-like bill that looks oversized for their petite frame

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in tight, fast-moving flocks that twist and turn in unison, wings beating rapidly with those blue patches flashing like strobes

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Males give a high, whistled 'peep' or 'tsee' sound, while females make a soft quacking that's higher-pitched than a mallard's hearty quack

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Tips forward to dabble and filter-feed at the water's surface, often in shallow areas where you can see their orange legs paddling

habitat: Look for blue-winged teal in shallow freshwater wetlands like marshes, ponds, and the quiet backwaters of rivers and streams. They prefer areas with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges, and are often found in smaller, more secluded wetlands rather than large open lakes. During migration, they'll use temporary flooded fields, beaver ponds, and constructed wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Migrants arrive in April and early May, with males showing their distinctive white facial crescents and courtship behaviors in shallow wetlands.
seasonality.summer: Breeding pairs nest in nearby grasslands while continuing to feed in wetlands. Young ducklings appear in late June and July.
seasonality.fall: Among the earliest duck migrants, many begin heading south by late August and September, though some pass through into October during peak migration.
seasonality.winter: Most have departed for warmer climates, though occasional stragglers may linger into early winter in milder years or protected coastal areas.

funFact: Blue-winged teal are incredible long-distance travelers despite their small size - some individuals migrate over 7,000 miles from their breeding grounds in Canada all the way to South America, making them one of the longest-distance migrants among North American ducks.
confusionNotes: Green-winged teal are the main confusion species, but they have green (not blue) wing patches and males have a green ear patch instead of a white facial crescent. Remember: 'Blue-wing, white crescent moon; green-wing, green ear patch.'
compareHints: Blue-winged teal are much smaller and more delicate than their cousin the Northern Shoveler, which has an enormous spoon-shaped bill and males show bright blue wing patches but with distinctive white chest patches and rusty sides. Blue-winged teal lack the oversized 'shovel' bill and have more subtle, mottled brown plumage overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relative the Blue-winged Teal which has a normal-sized, narrow bill perfect for picking at seeds, the Northern Shoveler's massive spatula bill is specialized for filter-feeding on microscopic organisms.
Unlike its close relative the blue-winged teal, male garganeys have that signature white eyebrow stripe instead of a white crescent on the face.
